title: Holy, holy, holy
hook: Isaiah sees the seraphim calling: holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:1–3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the still small voice, and Elijah hearing the quiet after the fire. Your line was still small voice. What did you hear when one noise went off? Today, the opposite: a vision full of sound. Day one thousand four.

Isaiah dates his vision by a king's death. In the King James words: "In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple." A king has died. And in the temple, Isaiah sees something that fills the room past its edges: the hem of a robe so vast it pours through the whole building. Above the throne stand the seraphim. Today, the word they keep calling to each other, three times over.
screen: `THE YEAR THE KING DIED.` → `HIS TRAIN FILLED THE TEMPLE.` → `THE SERAPHIM.`

segments.voice: First, the seraphim. The text describes them carefully: "each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly." Even these beings cover their faces. Awe, in Isaiah, isn't staring. It's knowing you can't quite look. Second, the call: "And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts". Not once. Three times, back and forth, as if once couldn't hold it. In Hebrew the word is qadosh. Jewish prayer takes up these words in the Kedushah, and Christian worship sings them in the Sanctus. Third, the second half of the line, the one that's easy to miss: "the whole earth is full of his glory." The holiness isn't kept inside the temple. It spills out, all the way to the edges of the world. Which means the street outside the temple, the market, the field, a kitchen, could all be places where that glory sits. Fourth, the human answer. Isaiah doesn't say how wonderful. He says: "Woe is me! for I am undone". Undone: in the old English sense, ruined, come apart. In the story, one of the seraphim flies to him with a live coal from the altar, touches his lips, and his sin is purged. Awe here takes him apart before it puts him back together. For anyone on this path, the seraphim's line leaves a question: what would it be like to call one ordinary thing holy, and mean it?
screen: `EVEN THE SERAPHIM COVER THEIR FACES.` · `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` · `THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL.` · `WOE IS ME: UNDONE.` · then, large: `HOLY.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Look around and choose one ordinary thing in reach: a cup, a key, your own hand, a window, a chair. Rest your eyes on it. Notice where it came from, who made it, what it has carried or held. Then, quietly or just inside, say one word over it: holy. Not because it's special. Because the seraphim said the whole earth is full, and this is a piece of the earth. Say it once, and let it sit. If you pray, you can say the seraphim's words themselves. If the word feels too big, just look at the thing a little longer. The bell holds the time.
Holy. In Hebrew, qadosh: the word the seraphim call to each other three times in Isaiah's vision, with the whole earth full of glory. Today's word.
Your line: holy, holy, holy. Pick three ordinary things today, one in the morning, one at noon, one at night, and say the word once over each. Day one thousand four.

howItsDone: Jews say the seraphim's words in the Kedushah, part of the repeated Amidah prayer, and Christians sing them in the Sanctus at the Eucharist; both come from Isaiah 6:3.

original.note: Hebrew: holy. the seraphim call it three times in Isaiah 6:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy means very good, or very religious.
what it means: so far beyond us the seraphim cover their faces, and its glory fills the earth.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah dates the vision to a king's death year, and answers it with: I am undone.

notes: Liturgy claims (Kedushah in the repeated Amidah; Sanctus at the Eucharist) are not in the cited text; Jewish and Christian Keepers should confirm wording.
Hook: 'the hem of a robe' reads KJV 'train'; framing.
'Undone, like a knot coming loose' is an image for the English word, not a claim about the Hebrew (nidmeti).
Hebrew qadosh spelling/transliteration to check. For a Jewish reader, JPS 1917 may be preferred for Isaiah 6.

Audit: 'undone, like a knot coming loose' was an image built on the English word, not Isaiah's Hebrew (nidmeti, roughly ruined or silenced); now glossed by the KJV-era sense, ruined. Match pair 'the seraphims' (KJV plural) changed to 'seraphim' to match the teach. Hook's 'above it' clarified to the throne.

Editor: 'creatures of fire' cut (rests on an etymology of seraph not in the text); 'by a funeral' to 'by a king's death' (6:1 names no funeral); 'an angel' corrected to 'one of the seraphim' with the live coal and purged sin as in Isaiah 6:6-7.
